titleEn: Suspected Opioid Overdose - Ventilate First, Then Naloxone

patient.name: Jordan Miles
patient.affectEn: at first completely unresponsive, lying on his back in a hallway, lips blue, chest barely moving; after naloxone he wakes confused and irritable, tries to pull off the oxygen mask and vomits
patient.speechEn: no speech at all while unresponsive (history comes from building staff and a resident). After naloxone: short, irritable, slightly confused answers; cooperative if spoken to calmly.

scene.settingEn: Single-room-occupancy hotel in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside, 0210 hrs. Dim, narrow hallway with worn carpet; room temperature about 20 degrees C. Building staff hold the door. The patient lies on his back on the hallway floor. Beside him: a used syringe with the needle exposed and a piece of foil. Two other residents watch from a doorway; they are not aggressive. Police are en route but not yet on scene. One patient.
hazardsEn: used syringe with an exposed needle beside the patient - a genuine sharps hazard that must be managed before kneeling or working over him
two residents watching from a doorway (not aggressive); police not yet on scene

bystanders.knowsEn: Found him down in the hallway roughly 5 minutes before calling 911 for help. He was 'barely breathing' and blue around the lips. Did not see him fall, no trauma seen, no seizure seen. Is holding the door and will help with doors or lighting if asked. Does not know his medical history.

bystanders.who: resident (one of the two in the doorway)
bystanders.knowsEn: Saw him smoke off foil and then inject about 20 minutes ago. Believes it was 'down' (fentanyl-contaminated). He was alone in the hallway when he used. No fall, no seizure seen. Does not know his medications or allergies.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: bag-valve mask with oxygen reservoir and tubing
oxygen kit with non-rebreather mask and nasal cannula
naloxone for IM injection with syringes and IM needles, and intranasal naloxone
PCP only: IV start kit with normal saline

dispatchEn: 0210 hrs. Code 3 to a single-room-occupancy hotel in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside. 31-year-old male found unresponsive in a hallway by building staff. Police are en route but not yet on scene. Hospital is 7 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: staff report he is 'barely breathing' and blue around the lips. A bystander says he used 'down' about 20 minutes ago.
arrivalEn: Building staff hold the front door and lead you down a dim, narrow hallway with worn carpet. A man lies on his back on the floor. Right beside him is a used syringe with the needle exposed and a piece of foil. Two residents watch from a doorway; they are not aggressive. Police are not on scene yet. Room temperature. One patient.
firstLookEn: A 31-year-old man on his back on the hallway floor, lips blue, chest barely moving, snoring sounds. He does not react to your arrival. A used syringe with an exposed needle and a piece of foil lie right beside his arm.

primary.locEn: Unresponsive: no response to voice and no response to a trapezius pinch (AVPU = U). He cannot protect his own airway.
primary.airwayEn: Snoring respirations, with vomit residue at the corner of the mouth - the airway needs SUCTION. Once suctioned, an OPA is tolerated (no gag reflex).
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 4 per minute, shallow and ineffective - inadequate; the chest barely moves. (Once BVM ventilations are started and chest rise is confirmed, the chest rises with each ventilation.)
primary.circulationEn: Carotid pulse 116, weak. Radial pulse absent. No external bleeding.
primary.rbsEn: Modified rapid body survey: no trauma, no medical alert; PINPOINT PUPILS; a fresh injection site in the left antecubital fossa. Skin cyanotic centrally, pale and cool peripherally (skin is given automatically during the RBS). No trauma and no fall witnessed - c-spine is not indicated once this has been checked.
primary.skinEn: cyanotic centrally, pale and cool peripherally

history.ccEn: (Before naloxone he cannot answer. Building staff: "We found him like this - he's barely breathing and his lips are blue.") After naloxone: "What happened? ... I used. I must have gone down."

opqrst.oEn: (Before naloxone - resident: "He smoked off the foil and then injected, about 20 minutes ago." Staff: "We found him down about 5 minutes before we called.") After naloxone: "I used in the hallway, by myself."
opqrst.pEn: (He cannot answer while unresponsive. Bystanders: "Nothing - he just went down.") After naloxone: "I don't know. Nothing."
opqrst.qEn: (He cannot answer while unresponsive.) After naloxone: "I feel sick. Short of breath."
opqrst.rEn: (He cannot answer while unresponsive.) After naloxone: "No, nothing like that."
opqrst.sEn: (He cannot answer while unresponsive.) After naloxone: "I feel awful."
opqrst.tEn: (Resident: "He used about 20 minutes ago." Staff: "Found him about 5 minutes before we called 911 for help.")

history.painScoreEn: (He cannot answer while unresponsive.) After naloxone he does not give a number: "I don't hurt. I just feel sick." (No numeric pain score is given in this scenario.)

sample.sEn: (Bystanders: "Barely breathing, blue lips.") After naloxone: "I feel sick, short of breath, my head hurts."
sample.aEn: (Bystanders do not know.) After naloxone: "No allergies."
sample.mEn: (Bystanders do not know.) After naloxone: "Nothing prescribed. I'm not on methadone or anything like that."
sample.pEn: (Bystanders do not know.) After naloxone: "Hep C. I've overdosed before - I've been revived twice. I had asthma as a kid."
sample.lEn: (Bystanders do not know.) After naloxone: "Three beers tonight. Food yesterday afternoon."
sample.eEn: (Resident: "He smoked off the foil and then injected - it was 'down' - about 20 minutes ago. No fall, no seizure.") After naloxone: "I used alone, here in the hallway. Nothing else tonight except the 3 beers. I've used every day for 3 years."

fe.generalEn: I've lost weight. I sleep rough some nights.
fe.cnsEn: My head hurts now. No seizure. No weakness anywhere.
fe.respiratoryEn: I feel short of breath and sick since I woke up.
fe.giGuEn: I feel like I'm going to throw up.
fe.integumentaryEn: Old track marks. That's where I just used, on my left arm.

findings.headNeckEn: No trauma, no tongue biting. Vomit residue at the mouth (cleared once suctioned). No neck stiffness. Pupils pinpoint and equal before naloxone; 3 mm and reactive after naloxone.
findings.chestLungsEn: Clear and equal at all 6 sites once he is being ventilated; no crackles.
findings.backEn: No injury (checked with a careful roll while ventilations are maintained).
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Track marks. No injury. No needle in situ.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: Fresh injection site in the left antecubital fossa; old track marks on both arms. Circulation, sensation and movement intact.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: baseline with ventilations in progress, before naloxone (BGL is mandatory before naloxone)

resp.character: spontaneous rate 4, ineffective; assisted with BVM at 10 per minute

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: about 4 minutes after naloxone 0.4 mg, en route; awake, confused and irritable, vomiting

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: He is still barely breathing; his lips are still blue and his chest is hardly moving.
He opens his eyes to your voice, confused and irritable, and tries to pull off the mask. He is vomiting.
He wakes abruptly, combative, pushes the mask away and says he is not going anywhere. He refuses care.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge; plan BVM with oxygen, suction, OPA/NPA, naloxone, glucometer
Anticipate respiratory failure - ventilation is the priority, not the drug
Verbalize hazards - exposed needle and drug paraphernalia, dim confined hallway, bystanders, police not yet on scene
ACT on the sharps hazard: move or safely dispose of the needle before working over the patient
triggers: secure the sharps before I kneel

expected.actionEn: Don gloves and eye protection (splash and airway secretions)
First look: cyanotic lips, minimal chest movement, drug paraphernalia beside him
Assess LOC / AVPU: Unresponsive - this patient cannot protect his own airway
Verbalize c-spine not indicated (no trauma found, no fall witnessed) after a deliberate check
Open the airway, SUCTION the vomit (10-15 seconds in an adult) and insert a correctly sized OPA
Recognize inadequate respirations and BEGIN ASSISTED VENTILATIONS IMMEDIATELY - this is the single most important action of the station
Use the C-A-B approach for the unconscious patient and check the carotid pulse
Modified rapid body survey: look for trauma, injection sites, patches and paraphernalia
Note skin: central cyanosis, cool and pale peripherally
Deliver oxygen via the BVM to bring SpO2 to 94 percent or above
Position supine for ventilation; do NOT place a patient requiring assisted respirations in the recovery position
triggers: flat on his back to ventilate

expected.actionEn: Use two-person BVM technique with the partner, confirming an effective seal and chest rise
Categorize as RTC and act with urgency
Ready to load within 15 minutes with ventilations maintained throughout the move
Maintain RTC status even if he wakes - verbalize the risk of re-sedation as naloxone wears off
triggers: still RTC even though he's awake
he needs to go to hospital

expected.actionEn: Establish chief complaint: unresponsiveness with respiratory depression, suspected opioid overdose
HxC/C from bystanders: substance, route, time of use, time found down, co-ingestants, previous overdoses
triggers: how long has he been down

expected.actionEn: PMHx (hepatitis C, previous overdoses, asthma)
Medications incl opioid agonist therapy status
Allergies
LOI incl alcohol
GCS with components (E1 V1 M1 = 3)
BP by auscultation
Pulse - assess the carotid when the radial is absent, and state rate, strength and rhythm
Respirations - rate, depth and effectiveness both spontaneous and assisted
Skin hands-on
Pupils - identify pinpoint pupils as an opioid sign
SpO2 with calibration; document the improvement with ventilation
triggers: sats are coming up with the bagging

expected.actionEn: BGL - explicitly required by the Narcotic Overdose protocol
Temperature - hypothermia is a listed feature of opioid overdose
FE - General health
FE - CNS
FE - Respiratory (pertinent)
FE - Cardiovascular
FE - GI/GU (vomiting risk after naloxone)
triggers: are you going to throw up

expected.actionEn: FE - Integumentary (injection sites)
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT
Head/neck exam incl airway clearance and trauma screen
Chest exam with 6-site auscultation - screen for aspiration and pulmonary edema
Abdomen exam
Back exam
triggers: roll him to check the back

expected.actionEn: Lower extremities - check for concealed needles before palpating
Upper extremities - injection sites and CSM
triggers: injection site in the left arm

expected.actionEn: Assist ventilations BEFORE giving naloxone - ventilation is the life-saving intervention
Obtain a BGL before or alongside naloxone as the protocol requires, and correct it if 4 mmol/L or less
triggers: sugar is 5.9 so no glucose needed
check the sugar before the Narcan

expected.actionEn: Naloxone 0.4 mg IM/IV with the 6 rights, correct site and needle
Verbalize the escalation schedule: repeat at 3-minute intervals 0.4, 0.8 then 2.0 mg if SpO2 94 percent or above and rate above 10 are not achieved
triggers: if sats aren't 94 and rate isn't above 10

expected.actionEn: Airway skill: suction correctly, size and insert the OPA properly, keep suction at hand for post-naloxone vomiting
triggers: measure from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe
he may vomit after the Narcan

expected.actionEn: Ventilation skill: BVM connected to oxygen, good seal, 8-10 breaths per minute, chest rise confirmed, no hyperventilation
Reassess ABCs and interventions after naloxone and after every change in LOC
triggers: his LOC changed so I'm rechecking ABCs
is he breathing on his own now

expected.actionEn: Second full set of vitals within 5-6 minutes, including a repeat pupil check
Manage post-naloxone vomiting: suction and airway positioning immediately
triggers: roll him on his side to clear the vomit
turn him to drain the airway

expected.actionEn: De-escalate agitation professionally and keep the patient monitored; maintain RTC status because of the re-sedation risk
triggers: you overdosed and we gave you naloxone
you need to come to hospital

expected.actionEn: En-route notification stating that the apneic patient was ventilated
Complete hand-off with naloxone dose/route/time, ventilation support and re-sedation risk
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate starts (or has the partner start) assisted ventilations with a BVM / bag-valve mask

candidate gives (or has the partner give) naloxone while the patient's inadequate respirations are NOT yet being assisted with a BVM - i.e. ventilations have not been started at or before the time of the naloxone
candidate kneels beside, works over, or moves the patient without first moving the exposed needle out of the way or disposing of it in a sharps container
candidate places the patient in the recovery / lateral position while he still requires assisted ventilations (before he is breathing adequately on his own)

candidate gives a naloxone dose outside the BC ladder: a first dose larger than 0.4 mg IM/IV (or other than 4 mg IN), a repeat dose larger than the next step (0.4 -> 0.4 -> 0.8 -> 2.0 mg), or a skipped step
candidate hyperventilates the patient: rate clearly and repeatedly far above 8-10 breaths per minute, or rapid continuous squeezing of the bag
after he wakes, candidate accepts his refusal, leaves him on scene, or downgrades him to non-urgent transport because he is awake (ignoring the re-sedation risk)

drugs.doseEn: 0.4 mg IM or IV; then 0.4 mg after 3 minutes, 0.8 mg after a further 3 minutes, 2.0 mg after a further 3 minutes - each repeat only if SpO2 >= 94% and ventilating > 10 have not been achieved; 4 mg IN. Only after ventilations are assisted and a baseline set of vitals including BGL. Target is adequate ventilation, not full arousal. PCP: IV route in continued unconsciousness and apnea.
drugs.indicationsEn: respiratory depression / depressed mental status secondary to actual or suspected narcotic use (decreased LOC, respirations 4 and ineffective, pinpoint pupils)
drugs.cautionsEn: patient combativeness; may precipitate withdrawal symptoms

drugs.doseEn: NOT indicated - BGL is 5.9 mmol/L (correction only if 4 mmol/L or less); oral glucose must never be given to an unresponsive patient - withhold

deduct.errorEn: Determines absent or irregular respirations but does not intervene immediately - this includes the primary survey and subsequent checks in the vital signs and ABC reassessments.
Determines absent or irregular respirations but does not intervene immediately - this includes the primary survey and subsequent checks in the vital signs and ABC reassessments.
Fails to administer a medication indicated by the protocol detrimental to patient care
Does not complete baseline vital signs prior to initiating the protocol
Does not sufficiently assess the patient to determine appropriate treatment (e.g. only assessing LOC to determine the need for Narcan)
Does not sufficiently assess the patient to determine appropriate treatment (e.g. only assessing LOC to determine the need for Narcan)
Gives incorrect dose/volume of drug or fluid
Performs the protocol with isolated error with potential to be detrimental to patient care
Initiated protocol without proper indications (e.g. patient is not DLOC)
Identifies a hazard during the SA but fails to act to make the scene safe
Positions the patient incorrectly detrimental to patient care
Ventilates at a rate not appropriate for patient
Does not perform an act that was required based on patient presentation that is potentially detrimental to patient care

notificationFacts.hxcc: witnessed to smoke off foil and then inject suspected fentanyl-contaminated 'down' about 20 minutes before; found down roughly 5 minutes before the 911 call; previous overdoses

notificationFacts.findings: pinpoint pupils resolving to 3 mm reactive; fresh injection site left antecubital fossa; vomiting since waking; re-sedation risk

handoffFacts.cc: found unresponsive with respiratory depression in an SRO hallway - suspected opioid overdose
handoffFacts.hxcc: found at approximately 0205; witnesses saw him smoke and then inject what is believed to be fentanyl-contaminated down about 20 minutes before; used alone; daily use for 3 years; revived twice before; 3 beers tonight, no other drugs
handoffFacts.initialVitals: GCS 3 (E1 V1 M1), respirations 4 and ineffective (assisted at 10), carotid 116 weak, radial absent, BP 96/58, skin cyanotic centrally, cool and pale peripherally, pupils pinpoint and equal, SpO2 72% rising to 96% with ventilation, BGL 5.9, temperature 35.8
handoffFacts.finalVitals: 4 minutes after naloxone: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), respirations 16 spontaneous and adequate, BP 118/70, pulse 104 regular with a palpable radial, skin pink warm dry, pupils 3 mm and reactive, SpO2 97% on oxygen, BGL 5.9, temperature 35.9
handoffFacts.pmhx: hepatitis C, previous overdoses, childhood asthma
handoffFacts.meds: none prescribed; not on opioid agonist therapy
handoffFacts.treatments: needle secured before patient contact; vomit suctioned and OPA inserted; two-person BVM ventilations with oxygen at 10 per minute bringing SpO2 to 96%; BGL checked before naloxone; naloxone 0.4 mg IM at 0219; suction kept at hand for post-naloxone vomiting
handoffFacts.findings: pinpoint pupils now 3 mm reactive; fresh injection site left antecubital fossa, old track marks; chest clear at 6 sites; has vomited once since waking; remains RTC because naloxone wears off before the opioid does (re-sedation risk)

examinerPrompts.locNotDepictedEn: He is unresponsive: no response to your voice and no response to the trapezius pinch.
examinerPrompts.breathingNotDepictedEn: His own breathing is very slow, shallow and ineffective - the chest barely moves and his lips are blue.

trackNotes.emrEn: EMR gives naloxone 0.4 mg IM (or 4 mg IN) on the same escalation schedule, with ventilation, suction, OPA/NPA and oxygen. EMR does not establish IV access, so persistent apnea is managed with continued BVM ventilation, repeat IM doses and rapid transport. No Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP may establish vascular access and give naloxone intravenously in continued unconsciousness and apnea (IV onset 1 minute versus 3 minutes IM). PCP also completes the Functional Enquiry once the patient can answer (no deduction for systems he cannot answer while unresponsive). The titration target is unchanged: adequate ventilation, not full arousal.

sourcePages: Scenario md-04 (data/practical/scenarios.json): dispatch, scene (exposed needle), primary, transport, history, vitals sets 1-2, FE, exam, interventions, ongoing, handoff. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (altered LOC / unconsciousness, respiratory distress / respiratory arrest = unstable); p.50 Oxygen Administration (consider assisted ventilations); p.52 PEEP use (ventilate usually no more than 8-10 breaths per minute); p.56 Suspected Narcotic Overdose (airway with positioning, suction and adjuncts; support ventilations, consider two-person BVM; SpO2 >= 94%; history and baseline vitals including BGL; correct glucose if <= 4 mmol/L; administer naloxone; transport and continue en route; PCP: vascular access and IV naloxone in continued unconsciousness and apnea); p.72 Naloxone (0.4 mg IM/IV, then 0.4 mg, 0.8 mg and 2.0 mg each after 3 minutes if SpO2 >= 94% and ventilating > 10 have not been achieved; 4 mg IN; onset IV 1 minute, IM/IN 3 minutes; cautions combativeness and withdrawal).
